content.content:
# Serial Data Transfer (Link Cable)

Communication between two Game Boy systems happens one byte at a time. One
Game Boy generates a clock signal internally and thus controls when the
exchange happens. In SPI terms, the Game Boy generating the clock is
called the "master" while the other one (the "slave" Game Boy) receives it.
If it hasn't gotten around to loading up the next
data byte at the time the transfer begins, the last one will go out
again. Alternately, if it's ready to send the next byte but the last
one hasn't gone out yet, it has no choice but to wait.

## FF01 — SB: Serial transfer data

Before a transfer, it holds the next byte that will go out.

During a transfer, it has a blend of the outgoing and incoming bytes.
Each cycle, the leftmost bit is shifted out (and over the wire) and the
incoming bit is shifted in from the other side:

{{#bits 8 >
   "Initially" 7:"o.7" 6:"o.6" 5:"o.5" 4:"o.4" 3:"o.3" 2:"o.2" 1:"o.1" 0:"o.0" ;
   "1 shift"  7:"o.6" 6:"o.5" 5:"o.4" 4:"o.3" 3:"o.2" 2:"o.1" 1:"o.0" 0:"i.7" ;
   "2 shifts" 7:"o.5" 6:"o.4" 5:"o.3" 4:"o.2" 3:"o.1" 2:"o.0" 1:"i.7" 0:"i.6" ;
   "3 shifts" 7:"o.4" 6:"o.3" 5:"o.2" 4:"o.1" 3:"o.0" 2:"i.7" 1:"i.6" 0:"i.5" ;
   "4 shifts" 7:"o.3" 6:"o.2" 5:"o.1" 4:"o.0" 3:"i.7" 2:"i.6" 1:"i.5" 0:"i.4" ;
   "5 shifts" 7:"o.2" 6:"o.1" 5:"o.0" 4:"i.7" 3:"i.6" 2:"i.5" 1:"i.4" 0:"i.3" ;
   "6 shifts" 7:"o.1" 6:"o.0" 5:"i.7" 4:"i.6" 3:"i.5" 2:"i.4" 1:"i.3" 0:"i.2" ;
   "7 shifts" 7:"o.0" 6:"i.7" 5:"i.6" 4:"i.5" 3:"i.4" 2:"i.3" 1:"i.2" 0:"i.1" ;
   "8 shifts" 7:"i.7" 6:"i.6" 5:"i.5" 4:"i.4" 3:"i.3" 2:"i.2" 1:"i.1" 0:"i.0"
}}

## FF02 — SC: Serial transfer control

{{#bits 8 >
   "SC" 7:"Transfer enable" 1:"Clock speed" 0:"Clock select"
}}

- **Transfer enable** (*Read/Write*): If `1`, a transfer is either requested or in progress.
- **Clock speed** \[*CGB Mode only*\] (*Read/Write*): If set to `1`, enable high speed serial clock (~256 kHz in normal-speed mode)
- **Clock select** (*Read/Write*): `0` = External clock ("slave"), `1` = Internal clock ("master").

The master Game Boy will load up a data byte in SB and then set
SC to \$81 (Transfer requested, use internal clock). It will be notified
that the transfer is complete in two ways: SC's Bit 7 will be cleared, and a [Serial interrupt](<#INT $58 — Serial interrupt>)
will be requested. When checking SC to determine if the transfer is complete, make sure to only read SC's Bit 7.

The other Game Boy will load up a data byte and has to set SC's
Bit 7 (that is, SC=\$80) to enable the serial port. The externally clocked
Game Boy will have a [serial interrupt](<#INT $58 — Serial interrupt>) requested at the end of the
transfer, and SC's Bit 7 will be cleared.

### Internal Clock

In Non-CGB Mode the Game Boy supplies an internal clock of 8192Hz only
(allowing to transfer about 1 KByte per second minus overhead for delays).
In CGB Mode four internal clock rates are available, depending on Bit 1
of the SC register, and on whether the CGB Double Speed Mode is used:

Clock freq | Transfer speed | Conditions
-----------|----------------|------------
   8192 Hz |     1 KB/s     | Bit 1 cleared, Normal speed
  16384 Hz |     2 KB/s     | Bit 1 cleared, Double-speed Mode
 262144 Hz |    32 KB/s     | Bit 1 set,     Normal speed
 524288 Hz |    64 KB/s     | Bit 1 set,     Double-speed Mode

### External Clock

The external clock is typically supplied by another Game Boy, but might
be supplied by another computer (for example if connected to a PC's
parallel port), in that case the external clock may have any speed. Even
the old/monochrome Game Boy is reported to recognize external clocks of
up to 500 kHz. And there is no limitation in the other direction: even
when suppling an external clock speed of "1 bit per month," the Game Boy
will eagerly wait for the next bit to be transferred. It isn't required
that the clock pulses are sent at a regular interval either.

## Timeouts

When using external clock then the transfer will not complete until the
last bit is received. In case that the second Game Boy isn't supplying a
clock signal, if it gets turned off, or if there is no second Game Boy
connected at all) then transfer will never complete. For this reason the
transfer procedure should use a timeout counter, and abort the
communication if no response has been received during the timeout
interval.

## Disconnects

On a disconnected link cable, the input bit on a master will start to read 1.
This means a master will start to receive $FF bytes.

If a disconnection happens during transmission, the input will be pulled up to 1 over a 20uSec period. (TODO: Only measured on a CGB rev E)
This means if the slave was sending a 0 bit at the time of the disconnect, you will read 0 bits for up to 20 μs.
Which, on a CGB at the highest speed, can amount to more than one byte.

## Delays and Synchronization

The master Game Boy should always execute a small
delay after each transfer, in order to ensure that the other
Game Boy has enough time to prepare itself for the next transfer. That is, the
Game Boy with external clock must have set its transfer start bit before
the Game Boy with internal clock starts the transfer. Alternately, the
two Game Boy systems could switch between internal and external clock for each
transferred byte to ensure synchronization.

Transfer is initiated when the master Game Boy sets its Transfer
Start Flag.
This bit is automatically set to 0 (on both) at the end of transfer.
Reading this bit can be used to determine if the transfer is still
active.
# Joypad Input

## FF00 — P1/JOYP: Joypad

The eight Game Boy action/direction buttons are arranged as a 2×4
matrix. Select either action or direction buttons by writing to this
register, then read out the bits 0-3.

{{#bits 8 >
  "P1" 5:"Select buttons" 4:"Select d-pad" 3:"Start / Down" 2:"Select / Up" 1:"B / Left" 0:"A / Right"
}}

- **Select buttons**: If this bit is `0`, then buttons (SsBA) can be read from the lower nibble.
- **Select d-pad**: If this bit is `0`, then directional keys can be read from the lower nibble.
- The lower nibble is *Read-only*.
  Note that, rather unconventionally for the Game Boy, a button being pressed is seen as the corresponding bit being **`0`**, not `1`.
  
  If neither buttons nor d-pad is selected (`$30` was written), then the low nibble reads `$F` (all buttons released).

:::tip NOTE

Most programs read from this port several times in a row
(the first reads are used as a short delay, allowing the inputs to stabilize,
and only the value from the last read is actually used).

:::

## Usage in SGB software

Beside for normal joypad input, SGB games misuse the joypad register to
output SGB command packets to the SNES, also, SGB programs may read out
gamepad states from up to four different joypads which can be connected
to the SNES. See SGB description for details.

# Serial Data Transfer (Link Cable)

Communication between two Game Boy systems happens one byte at a time. One
Game Boy generates a clock signal internally and thus controls when the
exchange happens. In SPI terms, the Game Boy generating the clock is
called the "master" while the other one (the "slave" Game Boy) receives it.

again. Alternately, if it's ready to send the next byte but the last
one hasn't gone out yet, it has no choice but to wait.

# OAM DMA Transfer

## FF46 — DMA: OAM DMA source address & start

Writing to this register starts a DMA transfer from ROM or RAM to OAM
(Object Attribute Memory).  The written value specifies the
transfer source address divided by $100, that is, source and destination are:

```
Source:      $XX00-$XX9F   ;XX = $00 to $DF
Destination: $FE00-$FE9F
```

The transfer takes 160 M-cycles: 640 dots (1.4 lines) in normal speed,
or 320 dots (0.7 lines) in CGB Double Speed Mode.
This is much faster than a CPU-driven copy.

## OAM DMA bus conflicts

On DMG, during OAM DMA, the CPU can access only HRAM (memory at $FF80-$FFFE).
For this reason, the programmer must copy a short procedure (see below) into HRAM, and use
this procedure to start the transfer **from inside HRAM**, and wait until
the transfer has finished.

On CGB, the cartridge and WRAM are on separate buses.
This means that the CPU can access ROM or cartridge SRAM during OAM DMA from WRAM, or WRAM during OAM DMA from ROM or SRAM.
However, because a `call` writes a return address to the stack, and the stack and variables are usually in WRAM,
it's still recommended to busy-wait in HRAM for DMA to finish even on CGB.

:::warning Interrupts

An interrupt writes a return address to the stack and fetches the interrupt handler's instructions from ROM.
Thus, it's critical to prevent interrupts during OAM DMA, especially in a program that uses timer, serial, or joypad interrupts, since they are not synchronized to the LCD.
This can be done by executing DMA within the VBlank interrupt handler or through the `di` instruction.

:::

While an OAM DMA is in progress, the PPU cannot read OAM properly either.
Thus, most programs execute DMA during [Mode 1](<#PPU modes>), inside or immediately after their VBlank handler.
But it is also possible to execute it during display redraw (Modes 2 and 3),
allowing to display more than 40 objects on the screen (that is, for
example 40 objects in the top half, and other 40 objects in the bottom half of
the screen), at the cost of a couple lines that lack objects.
If the transfer is started during Mode 3, graphical glitches may happen.

The details:

* If OAM DMA is active during OAM scan (mode 2), most PPU revisions read each object
  as being off-screen and thus hidden on that line.
* If OAM DMA is active during rendering (mode 3), the PPU reads whatever 16-bit word
  the DMA unit is writing to OAM when the object is fetched.
  This causes an incorrect tile number and attributes for objects already determined to be in range.

<!-- TODO: find Hacktix test ROM -->
<!-- TODO: keep working on "Red from OAM", a reproducer that races the beam to overwrite tile number and attributes of objects previously seen in Mode 2 -->

## Best practices

This 10-byte routine starts a transfer and waits for it to finish.
Many games copy a routine like it into HRAM and call it during Mode 1.

```rgbasm
run_dma:
    ld a, HIGH(start address)
    ldh [$FF46], a  ; start DMA transfer (starts right after instruction)
    ld a, 40        ; delay for a total of 4×40 = 160 M-cycles
.wait
    dec a           ; 1 M-cycle
    jr nz, .wait    ; 3 M-cycles
    ret
```

If HRAM is tight, this more compact procedure saves 5 bytes of HRAM
at the cost of a few M-cycles spent jumping to the tail in HRAM.

```rgbasm
run_dma:          ; This part must be in ROM.
    ld a, HIGH(start address)
    ld bc, $2846  ; B: wait time; C: LOW($FF46)
# Memory Map
The Game Boy has a 16-bit address bus, which is used to address ROM, RAM, and I/O.
Start       | End       | Description                                                      | Notes
------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------|----------
0000        | 3FFF      | 16 KiB ROM bank 00                                               | From cartridge, usually a fixed bank
4000        | 7FFF      | 16 KiB ROM Bank 01–NN                                            | From cartridge, switchable bank via [mapper](#MBCs) (if any)
8000        | 9FFF      | 8 KiB Video RAM (VRAM)                                           | In CGB mode, switchable bank 0/1
A000        | BFFF      | 8 KiB External RAM                                               | From cartridge, switchable bank if any
C000        | CFFF      | 4 KiB Work RAM (WRAM)                                            |
D000        | DFFF      | 4 KiB Work RAM (WRAM)                                            | In CGB mode, switchable bank 1–7
E000        | FDFF      | [Echo RAM](<#Echo RAM>) (mirror of C000–DDFF)                    | Nintendo says use of this area is prohibited.
FE00        | FE9F      | [Object attribute memory (OAM)](<#Object Attribute Memory (OAM)>) |
FEA0        | FEFF      | [Not Usable](<#FEA0–FEFF range>)                                 | Nintendo says use of this area is prohibited.
FF00        | FF7F      | [I/O Registers](<#I/O Ranges>)                                   |
FF80        | FFFE      | High RAM (HRAM)                                                  |
FFFF        | FFFF      | [Interrupt](#Interrupts) Enable register (IE)                    |
## I/O Ranges
The Game Boy uses the following I/O ranges:
Start   | End     | First appeared | Purpose
--------|---------|----------------|-------------
$FF00   |         |       DMG      | [Joypad input](<#FF00 — P1/JOYP: Joypad>)
$FF01   |  $FF02  |       DMG      | [Serial transfer](<#Serial Data Transfer (Link Cable)>)
$FF04   |  $FF07  |       DMG      | [Timer and divider](<#Timer and Divider Registers>)
$FF0F   |         |       DMG      | [Interrupts](<#FF0F — IF: Interrupt flag>)
$FF10   |  $FF26  |       DMG      | [Audio](<#Audio Registers>)
$FF30   |  $FF3F  |       DMG      | [Wave pattern](<#FF30–FF3F — Wave pattern RAM>)
$FF40   |  $FF4B  |       DMG      | LCD [Control](<#FF40 — LCDC: LCD control>), [Status](<#FF41 — STAT: LCD status>), [Position, Scrolling](<#Viewport position (Scrolling)>), and [Palettes](<#Palettes>)
$FF46   |         |       DMG      | [OAM DMA transfer](<#OAM DMA Transfer>)
$FF4C   |  $FF4D  |       CGB      | [KEY0](<#FF4C — KEY0/SYS (CGB Mode only): CPU mode select>) and [KEY1](<#FF4D — KEY1/SPD (CGB Mode only): Prepare speed switch>)
$FF4F   |         |       CGB      | [VRAM Bank Select](<#FF4F — VBK (CGB Mode only): VRAM bank>)
$FF50   |         |       DMG      | [Boot ROM mapping control](<#Power-Up Sequence>)
$FF51   |  $FF55  |       CGB      | [VRAM DMA](<#LCD VRAM DMA Transfers>)
$FF56   |         |       CGB      | [IR port](<#FF56 — RP (CGB Mode only): Infrared communications port>)
$FF68   |  $FF6B  |       CGB      | [BG / OBJ Palettes](<#LCD Color Palettes (CGB only)>)
$FF6C   |         |       CGB      | [Object priority mode](<#FF6C — OPRI (CGB Mode only): Object priority mode>)
$FF70   |         |       CGB      | [WRAM Bank Select](<#FF70 — SVBK/WBK (CGB Mode only): WRAM bank>)
## VRAM memory map
VRAM is, by itself, normal RAM, and may be used as such; however, the PPU interprets it in specific ways.
Bank 1 does not exist except on CGB, where it can be switched to (only in CGB Mode) using [the `VBK` register](<#FF4F — VBK (CGB Mode only): VRAM bank>).
Each bank first contains 384 tiles, of 16 bytes each.
These tiles are commonly thought of as grouped in three "blocks" of 128 tiles each; see [this detailed explanation](<#VRAM Tile Data>) for more details.
:::tip
The ID of a tile can be obtained from its address using the following equation:  
<var>ID</var> = <var>address</var> / 16 mod 256.
This is equivalent to only looking at the address' middle two hexadecimal digits.
:::
After the tiles, each bank contains two maps, 32×32 (= 1024) bytes each.
The two banks are however different here: bank 0 contains [tile maps](<#VRAM Tile Maps>), while bank 1 contains the corresponding [attribute maps](<#BG Map Attributes (CGB Mode only)>).
:::tip
Each entry corresponds to a set of coordinates, linked to its address:
- <var>X</var> = <var>address</var> mod 32
- <var>Y</var> = <var>address</var> / 32 mod 32
In fact, the address of any entry can be thought of as a bitfield:
{{#bits 16 >
	""  15:"1" 14:"0" 13:"0" 12:"1"  11:"1" 10:"<var>tilemap</var>" 9-5:"<var>Y</var>" 4-0:"<var>X</var>"
}}
:::
Here is a visualisation of how VRAM is laid out; hover over elements to see some details.
<noscript>
:::warning Interactive figure
Some of the information cannot be shown if JavaScript is disabled.
:::
</noscript>
{{#include imgs/src/vram_map.svg}}
<small>
The diagram is not to scale: each map takes up only half as much memory as a tile "block", despite the maps being visually twice as tall.
</small>
## Jump Vectors in first ROM bank
The following addresses are supposed to be used as jump vectors:
-   RST instructions: 0000, 0008, 0010, 0018, 0020, 0028, 0030, 0038
-   Interrupts: 0040, 0048, 0050, 0058, 0060
However, this memory area (0000-00FF) may be used for any other purpose in case that your
program doesn't use any (or only some) [`rst`](https://rgbds.gbdev.io/docs/gbz80.7#RST_vec) instructions or interrupts. `rst`
is a 1-byte instruction that works similarly to the 3-byte `call` instruction, except
that the destination address is restricted. Since it is 1-byte sized,
it is also slightly faster.
## Cartridge Header in first ROM bank
The memory area at 0100-014F contains the [cartridge
header](<#The Cartridge Header>). This area contains information
about the program, its entry point, checksums, information about the
used MBC chip, the ROM and RAM sizes, etc. Most of the bytes in this
area are required to be specified correctly.
## External Memory and Hardware
The areas from 0000-7FFF and A000-BFFF address external hardware on
the cartridge, which is essentially an expansion board.  Typically this
is a ROM and SRAM or, more often, a [Memory Bank Controller
(MBC)](#MBCs). The RAM area can be read
from and written to normally; writes to the ROM area control the MBC.
Some MBCs allow mapping of other hardware into the RAM area in this
way.
Cartridge RAM is often battery buffered to hold saved game positions,
high score tables, and other information when the Game Boy is turned
off.  For specific information read the chapter about [Memory Bank
Controllers](<#MBCs>).
## Echo RAM
The range E000-FDFF is mapped to WRAM, but only the lower 13 bits of
the address lines are connected, with the upper bits on the upper bank
set internally in the memory controller by a bank swap register.  This
causes the address to effectively wrap around.  All reads and writes to
this range have the same effect as reads and writes to C000-DDFF.

This can be done by executing DMA within the VBlank interrupt handler or through the `di` instruction.

:::

While an OAM DMA is in progress, the PPU cannot read OAM properly either.
Thus, most programs execute DMA during [Mode 1](<#PPU modes>), inside or immediately after their VBlank handler.
But it is also possible to execute it during display redraw (Modes 2 and 3),
allowing to display more than 40 objects on the screen (that is, for
example 40 objects in the top half, and other 40 objects in the bottom half of
the screen), at the cost of a couple lines that lack objects.
If the transfer is started during Mode 3, graphical glitches may happen.

The details:

* If OAM DMA is active during OAM scan (mode 2), most PPU revisions read each object
  as being off-screen and thus hidden on that line.
* If OAM DMA is active during rendering (mode 3), the PPU reads whatever 16-bit word
  the DMA unit is writing to OAM when the object is fetched.
  This causes an incorrect tile number and attributes for objects already determined to be in range.

## Best practices

This 10-byte routine starts a transfer and waits for it to finish.
Many games copy a routine like it into HRAM and call it during Mode 1.

```rgbasm
run_dma:
    ld a, HIGH(start address)
    ldh [$FF46], a  ; start DMA transfer (starts right after instruction)
    ld a, 40        ; delay for a total of 4×40 = 160 M-cycles
.wait
    dec a           ; 1 M-cycle
    jr nz, .wait    ; 3 M-cycles
    ret
```

If HRAM is tight, this more compact procedure saves 5 bytes of HRAM
at the cost of a few M-cycles spent jumping to the tail in HRAM.

```rgbasm
run_dma:          ; This part must be in ROM.
    ld a, HIGH(start address)
    ld bc, $2846  ; B: wait time; C: LOW($FF46)
# Memory Map
The Game Boy has a 16-bit address bus, which is used to address ROM, RAM, and I/O.
Start       | End       | Description                                                      | Notes
------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------------------------|----------
0000        | 3FFF      | 16 KiB ROM bank 00                                               | From cartridge, usually a fixed bank
4000        | 7FFF      | 16 KiB ROM Bank 01–NN                                            | From cartridge, switchable bank via [mapper](#MBCs) (if any)
8000        | 9FFF      | 8 KiB Video RAM (VRAM)                                           | In CGB mode, switchable bank 0/1
A000        | BFFF      | 8 KiB External RAM                                               | From cartridge, switchable bank if any
C000        | CFFF      | 4 KiB Work RAM (WRAM)                                            |
D000        | DFFF      | 4 KiB Work RAM (WRAM)                                            | In CGB mode, switchable bank 1–7
E000        | FDFF      | [Echo RAM](<#Echo RAM>) (mirror of C000–DDFF)                    | Nintendo says use of this area is prohibited.
FE00        | FE9F      | [Object attribute memory (OAM)](<#Object Attribute Memory (OAM)>) |
FEA0        | FEFF      | [Not Usable](<#FEA0–FEFF range>)                                 | Nintendo says use of this area is prohibited.
FF00        | FF7F      | [I/O Registers](<#I/O Ranges>)                                   |
FF80        | FFFE      | High RAM (HRAM)                                                  |
FFFF        | FFFF      | [Interrupt](#Interrupts) Enable register (IE)                    |
## I/O Ranges
The Game Boy uses the following I/O ranges:
Start   | End     | First appeared | Purpose
--------|---------|----------------|-------------
$FF00   |         |       DMG      | [Joypad input](<#FF00 — P1/JOYP: Joypad>)
$FF01   |  $FF02  |       DMG      | [Serial transfer](<#Serial Data Transfer (Link Cable)>)
$FF04   |  $FF07  |       DMG      | [Timer and divider](<#Timer and Divider Registers>)
$FF0F   |         |       DMG      | [Interrupts](<#FF0F — IF: Interrupt flag>)
$FF10   |  $FF26  |       DMG      | [Audio](<#Audio Registers>)
$FF30   |  $FF3F  |       DMG      | [Wave pattern](<#FF30–FF3F — Wave pattern RAM>)
$FF40   |  $FF4B  |       DMG      | LCD [Control](<#FF40 — LCDC: LCD control>), [Status](<#FF41 — STAT: LCD status>), [Position, Scrolling](<#Viewport position (Scrolling)>), and [Palettes](<#Palettes>)
$FF46   |         |       DMG      | [OAM DMA transfer](<#OAM DMA Transfer>)
$FF4C   |  $FF4D  |       CGB      | [KEY0](<#FF4C — KEY0/SYS (CGB Mode only): CPU mode select>) and [KEY1](<#FF4D — KEY1/SPD (CGB Mode only): Prepare speed switch>)
$FF4F   |         |       CGB      | [VRAM Bank Select](<#FF4F — VBK (CGB Mode only): VRAM bank>)
$FF50   |         |       DMG      | [Boot ROM mapping control](<#Power-Up Sequence>)
$FF51   |  $FF55  |       CGB      | [VRAM DMA](<#LCD VRAM DMA Transfers>)
$FF56   |         |       CGB      | [IR port](<#FF56 — RP (CGB Mode only): Infrared communications port>)
$FF68   |  $FF6B  |       CGB      | [BG / OBJ Palettes](<#LCD Color Palettes (CGB only)>)
$FF6C   |         |       CGB      | [Object priority mode](<#FF6C — OPRI (CGB Mode only): Object priority mode>)
$FF70   |         |       CGB      | [WRAM Bank Select](<#FF70 — SVBK/WBK (CGB Mode only): WRAM bank>)
## VRAM memory map
VRAM is, by itself, normal RAM, and may be used as such; however, the PPU interprets it in specific ways.
Bank 1 does not exist except on CGB, where it can be switched to (only in CGB Mode) using [the `VBK` register](<#FF4F — VBK (CGB Mode only): VRAM bank>).
Each bank first contains 384 tiles, of 16 bytes each.
These tiles are commonly thought of as grouped in three "blocks" of 128 tiles each; see [this detailed explanation](<#VRAM Tile Data>) for more details.
:::tip
The ID of a tile can be obtained from its address using the following equation:  
<var>ID</var> = <var>address</var> / 16 mod 256.
This is equivalent to only looking at the address' middle two hexadecimal digits.
:::
After the tiles, each bank contains two maps, 32×32 (= 1024) bytes each.
The two banks are however different here: bank 0 contains [tile maps](<#VRAM Tile Maps>), while bank 1 contains the corresponding [attribute maps](<#BG Map Attributes (CGB Mode only)>).
:::tip
Each entry corresponds to a set of coordinates, linked to its address:
- <var>X</var> = <var>address</var> mod 32
- <var>Y</var> = <var>address</var> / 32 mod 32
In fact, the address of any entry can be thought of as a bitfield:
{{#bits 16 >
	""  15:"1" 14:"0" 13:"0" 12:"1"  11:"1" 10:"<var>tilemap</var>" 9-5:"<var>Y</var>" 4-0:"<var>X</var>"
}}
:::
Here is a visualisation of how VRAM is laid out; hover over elements to see some details.
<noscript>
:::warning Interactive figure
Some of the information cannot be shown if JavaScript is disabled.
:::
</noscript>
{{#include imgs/src/vram_map.svg}}
<small>
The diagram is not to scale: each map takes up only half as much memory as a tile "block", despite the maps being visually twice as tall.
</small>
## Jump Vectors in first ROM bank
The following addresses are supposed to be used as jump vectors:
-   RST instructions: 0000, 0008, 0010, 0018, 0020, 0028, 0030, 0038
-   Interrupts: 0040, 0048, 0050, 0058, 0060
However, this memory area (0000-00FF) may be used for any other purpose in case that your
program doesn't use any (or only some) [`rst`](https://rgbds.gbdev.io/docs/gbz80.7#RST_vec) instructions or interrupts. `rst`
is a 1-byte instruction that works similarly to the 3-byte `call` instruction, except
that the destination address is restricted. Since it is 1-byte sized,
it is also slightly faster.
## Cartridge Header in first ROM bank
The memory area at 0100-014F contains the [cartridge
header](<#The Cartridge Header>). This area contains information
about the program, its entry point, checksums, information about the
used MBC chip, the ROM and RAM sizes, etc. Most of the bytes in this
area are required to be specified correctly.
## External Memory and Hardware
The areas from 0000-7FFF and A000-BFFF address external hardware on
the cartridge, which is essentially an expansion board.  Typically this
is a ROM and SRAM or, more often, a [Memory Bank Controller
(MBC)](#MBCs). The RAM area can be read
from and written to normally; writes to the ROM area control the MBC.
Some MBCs allow mapping of other hardware into the RAM area in this
way.
Cartridge RAM is often battery buffered to hold saved game positions,
high score tables, and other information when the Game Boy is turned
off.  For specific information read the chapter about [Memory Bank
Controllers](<#MBCs>).
## Echo RAM
The range E000-FDFF is mapped to WRAM, but only the lower 13 bits of
the address lines are connected, with the upper bits on the upper bank
set internally in the memory controller by a bank swap register.  This
causes the address to effectively wrap around.  All reads and writes to
this range have the same effect as reads and writes to C000-DDFF.

# Interrupts
## IME: Interrupt master enable flag \[write only\]
`IME` is a flag internal to the CPU that controls whether *any* interrupt handlers are called, regardless of the contents of `IE`.
`IME` cannot be read in any way, and is modified by these instructions/events only:
- **`ei`**: Enables interrupt handling (that is, `IME := 1`)
- **`di`**: Disables interrupt handling (that is, `IME := 0`)
- **`reti`**: Enables interrupts and returns (same as `ei` immediately followed by `ret`)
- **When an [interrupt handler](<#Interrupt handling>) is executed**: Disables interrupts before `call`ing the interrupt handler
`IME` is unset (interrupts are disabled) [when the game starts running](<#0100-0103 — Entry point>).
The effect of `ei` is delayed by one instruction. This means that `ei`
followed immediately by `di` does not allow any interrupts between them.
This interacts with the [`halt` bug](<#halt bug>) in an interesting way.
## FFFF — IE: Interrupt enable
{{#bits 8 >
  "IE" 4:"Joypad" 3:"Serial" 2:"Timer" 1:"LCD" 0:"VBlank"
}}
- **VBlank** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the VBlank interrupt handler](<#INT $40 — VBlank interrupt>) may be called (see `IF` below).
- **LCD** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the LCD interrupt handler](<#INT $48 — STAT interrupt>) may be called (see `IF` below).
- **Timer** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Timer interrupt handler](<#INT $50 — Timer interrupt>) may be called (see `IF` below).
- **Serial** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Serial interrupt handler](<#INT $58 — Serial interrupt>) may be called (see `IF` below).
- **Joypad** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Joypad interrupt handler](<#INT $60 — Joypad interrupt>) may be called (see `IF` below).
## FF0F — IF: Interrupt flag
{{#bits 8 >
  "IF" 4:"Joypad" 3:"Serial" 2:"Timer" 1:"LCD" 0:"VBlank"
}}
- **VBlank** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the VBlank interrupt handler](<#INT $40 — VBlank interrupt>) is being requested.
- **LCD** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the LCD interrupt handler](<#INT $48 — STAT interrupt>) is being requested.
- **Timer** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Timer interrupt handler](<#INT $50 — Timer interrupt>) is being requested.
- **Serial** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Serial interrupt handler](<#INT $58 — Serial interrupt>) is being requested.
- **Joypad** (*Read/Write*): Controls whether [the Joypad interrupt handler](<#INT $60 — Joypad interrupt>) is being requested.
When an interrupt request signal (some internal wire going from the PPU/APU/... to the CPU) changes from low to high, the corresponding bit in the `IF` register becomes set.
For example, bit 0 becomes set when the PPU enters the [VBlank](<#PPU modes>) period.
Any set bits in the `IF` register are only **requesting** an interrupt.
The actual **execution** of the interrupt handler happens only if both the `IME` flag and the corresponding bit in the `IE` register are set; otherwise the
interrupt "waits" until **both** `IME` and `IE` allow it to be serviced.
Since the CPU automatically sets and clears the bits in the `IF` register, it
is usually not necessary to write to the `IF` register. However, the user
may still do that in order to manually request (or discard) interrupts.
Just like real interrupts, a manually requested interrupt isn't serviced
unless/until `IME` and `IE` allow it.
## Interrupt handling
1. The `IF` bit corresponding to this interrupt and the `IME` flag are reset by the CPU.
The former "acknowledges" the interrupt, while the latter prevents any further interrupts
from being handled until the program re-enables them, typically by using the `reti` instruction.
2. The corresponding interrupt handler (see the `IE` and `IF` register descriptions [above](<#FFFF — IE: Interrupt enable>)) is
called by the CPU. This is a regular call, exactly like what would be performed by a `call <address>` instruction (the current PC is pushed onto the stack
and then set to the address of the interrupt handler).
The following interrupt service routine is executed when control is being transferred to an interrupt handler:
1. Two wait states are executed (2 M-cycles pass while nothing happens; presumably the CPU is executing `nop`s during this time).
2. The current value of the PC register is pushed onto the stack, consuming 2 more M-cycles.
3. The PC register is set to the address of the handler (one of: $40, $48, $50, $58, $60).
This consumes one last M-cycle.
The entire process [lasts 5 M-cycles](https://gist.github.com/SonoSooS/c0055300670d678b5ae8433e20bea595#user-content-isr-and-nmi).
## Interrupt priorities
In the following circumstances it is possible that more than one bit in the IF register is set, requesting more than one interrupt at once:
1. More than one interrupt request signal changed from low to high at the same time.
2. Several interrupts have been requested while IME/IE didn't allow them to be serviced.
3. The user has written a value with several bits set (for example binary 00011111) to the IF register.
If IME and IE allow the servicing of more than one of the
requested interrupts, the interrupt with the highest priority
is serviced first. The priorities follow the order of the bits in the IE
and IF registers: Bit 0 (VBlank) has the highest priority, and Bit 4
(Joypad) has the lowest priority.
## Nested interrupt handling
The CPU automatically disables all the other interrupts by setting IME=0
when it services an interrupt. Usually IME remains zero until the
interrupt handler returns (and sets IME=1 by means of the `reti` instruction).
However, if you want to allow the servicing of other interrupts (of any priority)
during the execution of an interrupt handler, you may do so by using the
`ei` instruction in the handler.

Since the deterministic roundtrip test holds no buttons between actions typically, I'll include button state anyway for full fidelity, since consistent button state across save/load keeps replay hashes matching.

For Timer I'm tracking the counter, TIMA, TMA, TAC, and a state enum, while Interrupts just need IF and IE flags. The Bus itself owns WRAM, HRAM, APU memory, and a cycle counter, with a version field for snapshot compatibility.

I'm structuring Bus::read and write so they tick the clock first then delegate to a shared read_mapped helper, keeping peek's logic consistent with the ticking reads.

Working through the timer's edge cases around TIMA overflow and reload timing — writes during the overflow cycle cancel the reload, while writes on the reload cycle itself get ignored, matching Mooneye's test expectations. I want to validate this against the known timer quirks (DIV write glitches, TAC-disable glitch) even though the main priority is getting Blargg's tests passing first.

For the glitch cases, I'm implementing a falling-edge detector: computing a signal from the masked counter bits ANDed with the TAC enable flag, and whenever that signal drops from 1 to 0 after any counter reset or TAC write, that triggers an extra TIMA increment — this covers both the DIV-write glitch and the TAC-disable glitch uniformly. I'm now thinking through how a write-triggered increment that causes TIMA to overflow interacts with the existing reload state machine, and how the falling-edge check composes with the regular per-tick increment logic.

I'm sketching the register read logic for the timer (DIV, TIMA, TMA, TAC with unused bits forced high) and noting the quirk that writing to TIMA during the overflow cycle suppresses the pending interrupt/reload. Then I move on to serial transfer: writing SC starts a transfer only if both the enable and internal-clock bits are set, arming a countdown of about 1024 M-cycles, and the tick handler decrements that countdown, firing completion logic once it reaches zero.

For serial completion, I set SB to 0xFF, clear the transfer bit in SC, and raise the serial interrupt, with the timing designed to land exactly 4096 T-cycles after the write — noting this is roughly aligned with Mooneye's boot_sclk_align tests but treating full accuracy as a later concern. Reads of SC/SB just return the stored bytes with unused bits forced high, and I add a helper to drain the collected output buffer.

Finally I move to joypad handling: storing the button select bits, computing the active nibble from pressed buttons, returning the standard 0xC0-padded read value, and detecting falling edges on the nibble during tick to trigger the joypad interrupt.

Now I'm thinking through Machine::new needing a fingerprint field alongside the Cpu and Bus setup with proper power-up I/O defaults (IF=0xE1, IE=0, etc.), building a synthetic 32KiB ROM with header byte 0x147=0x00 for testing, and considering how to validate step() and run_frame() timing — since an all-NOP ROM makes every step exactly 4 T whether using the real CPU or the stub, I realize I need variable-length instructions to properly test the 70224 T frame-boundary remainder accumulation.

I'm settling on a bounded-overshoot assertion (0 <= cycles - n*FRAME_T < 24) using an infinite loop of NOP + JP as the test ROM, since this works correctly for both the real CPU and the stub, and catches drift from lost remainder cycles across multiple frames. I could also add a #[cfg(test)] unit test directly in machine.rs to access the private frame_budget field for a more precise check.

Beyond that, I'll add a basic sanity check that Machine::step always returns a positive multiple of 4, and look into testing the Timer peripheral separately through the Bus or its own API in a dedicated timer test file.

For timer tests, I can write DIV to reset the internal counter to zero, then set TAC to enable the timer and control the increment frequency. I need to be careful about the order of writes since changing TAC or DIV while a particular counter bit is high can trigger a spurious TIMA increment, so I should think through the bit timing carefully to avoid flaky tests.

Still writing timer setup...

For the overflow test, I'm checking that TIMA resets to TMA and fires an interrupt when it wraps past 0xFF, verifying the timing matches the expected M-cycle delay.

I'm also tracing DIV register behavior across cycles, confirming that after a given number of ticks the upper byte of the internal counter matches the expected DIV value.

Right, core/src must stay free of any test-ROM naming, so I'll justify the DIV=$AB value by citing Pan Docs' documented boot state instead of referencing any specific test suite. The actual test files under crates/core/tests can still encode the derivation logic itself.

I should double check my cycle count: the first M-cycle after boot lands on PC=0x100 fetching the NOP opcode, which is a read access.

With tick-then-access, counter = c0 + 4k at the k-th access, so for k=14, c0 + 56 = 0xAC00 gives c0 = 0xABC8, matching. The DIV expectation for the boot_hwio test is harder to verify without a full instruction trace, so I'll skip that for now, and I notice Bus::new sets IF=0xE1.

For the APU region FF10–FF3F, since IE=0 at boot the pending VBlank flag in IF doesn't matter. I'm deciding on initial values: FF15/FF1F/FF27-FF2F should be 0xFF per the standard table, and I'll leave wave RAM contents unspecified since the boot_hwio test skips it anyway. I'm also weighing whether writing 0 to NR52 bit 7 should clear all APU registers, and whether games like Pokemon actually poll NR52's channel-on status bits when waiting for sound playback to finish.

I don't think Pokemon relies on that polling, so plain storage without special NR52 behavior should be safe. Now I'm mapping out the I/O dispatch logic: routing FF00 to joypad, FF01–FF02 to serial, FF04–FF07 to timer, FF0F to IF, FF10–FF3F to APU storage, FF40–FF45/FF47–FF4B to PPU, FF46 to DMA, and defaulting unmapped addresses to return 0xFF with writes ignored. I'm also handling FF50 (boot ROM disable) as a no-op, HRAM as a 0x7F-byte region at FF80–FFFE, ignoring writes to FEA0–FEFF, and making OAM reads return 0xFF when DMA blocks access -- with peek() sharing this same mapping as read().

I don't think peek access during OAM blocking matters much here. Now I'm sketching the Bus snapshot format (tag, wram, hram, apu, mcycles) and the Interrupts struct's accessor methods for IF/IE flags and interrupt requests/acknowledgment. I'm also planning CpuBus::stop to reset the DIV timer, checking whether the core lane has diverged from my worktree (though I don't need to sync since the integrator handles merging), and noting that Cpu::step is currently just an idle stub per the integrator's comment. I'm also thinking about keeping the F register's H/C flag rules as-is, deferring deeper analysis of instr_timing/mem_timing tests for the report, and confirming the bus's per-M-cycle tick (four peripheral ticks plus DMA) should be fine performance-wise before starting to sketch the Timer struct's fields.

Writing timer logic...

I'm now working out how writes to FF04-FF07 interact with the overflow/reload phase state, handling edge cases where TIMA, TMA, or TAC writes occur during the exact cycle of a pending reload, and checking whether a TAC write changes the signal state enough to trigger an immediate increment.

There's an apparent contradiction between sources on what happens when TMA is written during the overflow cycle B — one says the old value gets copied to TIMA, another says the new value does. I need to check the Mooneye tma_write_reloading test to figure out which behavior is actually correct.

I need to simulate this with the timer model to verify precisely. With TAC set so bit5 toggles every 64 T-cycles (16 M-cycles), and TIMA/TMA both at 0xFE, I'm tracing through the exact M-cycle timing of the DIV reset, the h-register load, the nop padding, and the TMA write to pin down when the counter edge actually lands.

Taking the second DIV write as cycle 0, the counter increments by 4 per M-cycle: the bit5 falling edge (overflow trigger) lands at k=16, giving TIMA FE→FF, then another edge at k=32 causing overflow and reload. Tracking the ld a,h, the 28 nops, and the TMA write through these M-cycle counts, I find the TMA write lands right around k=32 — directly overlapping the overflow cycle, which is the critical timing case I need to pin down.

For case d (TMA write at cycle A=32): the overflow phase hits exactly as TMA is written with 0x7F, and the subsequent read at k=35 confirms TIMA becomes 0x7F, matching expected $7f.

For case e (TMA write at cycle B=33, right after reload): the reload copies the old TMA into TIMA first, then the new TMA write of 0x7F still takes effect due to the Reloaded phase behavior, giving read result 0x7F — confirming expected $7f and validating the obscure timing quirk.

For case c (TMA write at k=34, after reload completes): TIMA stays at FE as read, matching expected $fe, and case l with nops totaling to k=35 also confirms TIMA=FE as expected.

I'm now double-checking my assumption about exactly when that first falling edge occurs, since the whole timing chain depends on getting that boundary right.

If I shifted the edge one cycle earlier, cases d and e would collide and give the same wrong result for e (FE instead of 7F), so the fact that my model produces distinct correct answers for both confirms the edge timing and the "tick then access" ordering I'm using are consistent with this test.

Now I want to quickly check the tima_write_reloading test case too, since it should be cheap to verify against the same model.

Game Boy CPU Instruction Timing Test
------------------------------------
This ROM tests the timings of all CPU instructions except HALT, STOP,
and the 11 illegal opcodes. For conditional instructions, it tests taken
and not taken timings. This test requires proper timer operation (TAC,
TIMA, TMA).

Failed instructions are listed as

	[CB] opcode:measured time-correct time

Times are in terms of instruction cycles, where NOP takes one cycle.


Verified cycle timing tables
----------------------------
The test internally uses a table of proper cycle times, which can be
used in an emulator to ensure proper timing. The only changes below are
removal of the .byte prefixes, and addition of commas at the ends, so
that they can be used without changes in most programming languages. For
added correctness assurance, the original tables can be found at the end
of the source code.

Normal instructions:

	1,3,2,2,1,1,2,1,5,2,2,2,1,1,2,1,
	0,3,2,2,1,1,2,1,3,2,2,2,1,1,2,1,
	2,3,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,2,2,1,1,2,1,
	2,3,2,2,3,3,3,1,2,2,2,2,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	2,2,2,2,2,2,0,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,
	1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,1,

; Initializes timer
; Preserved: AF, BC, DE, HL
init_timer:
     push af
     di
     lda  IE        ; disable timer interrupt
     and  ~$04
     sta  IE
     wreg TMA,0     ; max period
     wreg TAC,$05   ; 262144 Hz
     
     ; Be sure timer doesn't expire
     ; immediately or take too long
     wreg IF,0
     wreg TIMA,-20
     delay 70
     lda  IF
     and  $04
     jp   nz,test_failed
     lda  IF
     and  $04
     jp   z,test_failed

     pop  af
     ret


; Starts timer
; Preserved: AF, BC, DE, HL
start_timer:
     push af
     
-    xor  a         ; 1
     sta  TIMA      ; 3
     lda  TIMA      ; 3
     or   a         ; 1
     jr   nz,-      ; 3
     
     pop  af
     ret


; Stops timer and determines cycles since
; it was started. A = cycles (0 to 255).
; Preserved: BC, DE, HL
stop_timer:

     add  a
     rl   d
     add  a

     ld   e,a

-    xor  a         ; 1
     sta  TIMA      ; 3
     lda  TIMA      ; 3

I'm now updating machine.rs to add a fingerprint field and implement save_state/load_state, defining constants for a state file magic number, version, and fingerprint length, plus a function to compute a ROM fingerprint.

The save_state method writes a header followed by each subsystem's serialized state (CPU, bus, interrupts, timer, serial, joypad, PPU, DMA, cartridge) and the frame budget. For load_state, I'm having it validate the header against the stored fingerprint before touching any state, then back up the current state so I can restore it if loading the body fails partway through or leaves unread bytes, treating either case as corruption.

I'm now working out the magic-byte validation logic for check_header -- deciding whether a truncated or mismatched prefix should map to Truncated versus BadMagic errors, leaning toward returning BadMagic whenever the available bytes don't match the expected magic sequence.

Beyond that, I plan version mismatches to produce BadVersion and fingerprint mismatches to produce RomMismatch. If restoring the backup state itself fails, I'm treating that as a genuine bug worth panicking on, since each module's own load routine should be reliable for its own saved format, and I'm fine with calling save_state before every load given the performance is negligible.

Writing the snapshot sequence saves Cpu, Bus, Cart, then Machine::frame_budget in order, with the ld_b_b flag handled internally by Cpu. For Machine::new I'm keeping the rom.len() < 0x150 check and computing the fingerprint before passing the rom into from_rom.

For the bus tests, I'm planning to check each memory region: ROM reads/writes, VRAM read-back, cart RAM returning 0xFF when RomOnly has no RAM, WRAM writes with echo region mirroring, OAM read-back, the FEA0–FEFF unusable range, unused I/O registers returning 0xFF, APU register storage behavior including the NR52 power-up value, HRAM, IE, IF defaulting to 0xE0, and power-up register values like P1=CF.

For DMA, since the PPU stub returns None from tick, I can't fully test OAM DMA transfer yet — I'll write that test now but mark it #[ignore] with a note to enable once the real PPU lands, so it writes to FF46 and checks OAM contents after enough idle cycles.

For the Machine-level tests, I'm planning checks for power-up register values, step() returning 4 cycles for a NOP, run_frame advancing exactly 70224 T-cycles, peek not consuming cycles, and take_serial starting empty. The save_state test hits a snag though — it would call into Cpu::save which is still a todo!() panic, so I can only verify the header/magic/version/fingerprint path for now, not the full round-trip, until snapshot support is implemented in core.

For header validation failures (bad magic, bad version, ROM mismatch, truncated data), I can construct the bytes manually using a public `rom_fingerprint()` method I'm adding, and confirm these fail before touching the panicking save path — so those tests can run safely while the full round-trip stays marked `#[ignore]`. For the ROM mismatch case specifically, I'd build a header with a fingerprint from a different ROM title and verify the machine state (registers, cycles) stays unchanged after the failed load.

For a synthetic 32 KiB test ROM, I'm thinking through filling it mostly with NOPs so execution flows predictably past the header into VRAM and cart RAM reads, considering how RST 38 gets triggered by 0xFF reads and whether that still loops safely without crashing — though adding a `JP 0x0100` jump back near the header would make the loop cleaner and more controlled than relying on fallthrough into RAM reads.

Checking the low 2 bits claim holds since the counter resets to 0 and BOOT's value is already a multiple of 4. I'm also considering how DIV resets mid M-cycle, where the counter would keep ticking through the remaining T-states of that cycle after the write.

Now I'm planning out the timer test cases: DIV incrementing every 256 T-cycles, the power-up boot phase behavior, TIMA rates for each TAC setting (verifying increments at 4, 16, 64, and 256 T-cycle periods), confirming a disabled timer doesn't tick, and the glitch where writing DIV causes an extra TIMA increment depending on which counter bit was set beforehand.

I'm also working through the falling-edge glitch for TAC changes, checking cases where switching TAC values causes an extra TIMA increment versus no increment, including the Pan Docs example with counter $3FF0 and TAC transitions between $FC, $05, and $06.

Checking against Pan Docs: with TAC bit indices mapped, writing $05 (bit3=0) gives a tick, $06 maps to bit5 which is already 1 in my model, so no falling edge — meaning my bit-selection model disagrees with the documented behavior for $06, so I need to find where my reasoning diverges.

But if the system counter actually increments per M-cycle rather than T-cycle, DIV would read bits 6-13, and TAC would select bits 1/3/5/7 instead — testing that against $3FF0 makes all four Pan Docs claims line up correctly ($05 and $06 tick, $07 and $04 don't), so this M-cycle counting model seems right.

This means my T-cycle counter equivalent is just the M-counter shifted left by two, so I can construct the matching state by ticking from zero up to 0x3FF0 times in M-cycle terms, or 0xFFC0 in T-cycle terms — a bit wasteful but workable since I can't set the counter directly. I'm now checking the second Pan Docs example with TAC=$FD to see if it's consistent too.

Next I need to walk through the overflow and reload sequence with TMA=0x23, TIMA=0xFE, TAC=0x05, verifying the exact tick where TIMA increments, overflows to zero, and then reloads with the TMA value while firing the timer interrupt — matching the Pan Docs table step by step. Then I want to test the edge cases: writing TIMA during the overflow cycle cancels the reload and IRQ, writing TIMA during the reload cycle gets ignored, writing TMA during the reload cycle changes what TIMA becomes, and writing TMA one cycle earlier still affects the reload due to the old value being used in the transfer.

I'll replicate the tima_reload test timing exactly through bus calls: write DIV, then 28 idle cycles, then two fetch reads, then a TIMA read — matching Mooneye's expected d/e/c sequence through the timer_bus test.

I'm also setting up helpers for simulating opcode fetches and LDH read/write sequences, then mapping the boot DIV phase timing (nop + jp, then pushes and nops) through Bus calls with specific DIV value assertions at each step.

Now I'm designing the Serial struct for T16, tracking SB/SC registers and a countdown of M-cycles for internal-clock transfers, with 1024 cycles representing the 8192Hz transfer rate.

Writing SC with 0x81 triggers a transfer, pushing SB into the output buffer and restarting the countdown—matching Blargg's test ROM behavior where each write fires off a byte. For snapshots I'll tag it SERI and store sb, sc, and the remaining counter.

content.content:
Game Boy CPU Memory Access Timing Test
--------------------------------------
This ROM tests the timing of memory reads and writes made by
instructions, except stack and program counter accesses. These tests
require correct instruction timing and proper timer operation (TAC,
TIMA, TMA).

The read and write tests list failing instructions as

	[CB] opcode:tested-correct

The read-modify-write test lists failing instructions as 

	[CB] opcode:tested read/tested write-correct read/correct write

The values after the opcode refer to which instruction cycle the access
occurs on, with 1 being the first. If a time couldn't be determined due
to some other problem, it prints 0.

For instructions which either read or write, but not both, the CPU makes
the access on the last cycle. For instructions which read, modify, then
write back, the CPU reads on the next-to-last cycle, and writes on the
last cycle.


Internal operation
------------------
The tests have the timer increment TIMA every 64 cycles, synchronize
with this, delay a variable amount, then have the instruction under test
access the timer. By varying the delay in one-cycle increments, the
memory access made by the instruction can be made to fall before and
after a TIMA increment. By then examining the registers and value in
TIMA, it can be determined which occurred.


Multi-ROM
---------
In the main directory is a single ROM which runs all the tests. It
prints a test's number, runs the test, then "ok" if it passes, otherwise
a failure code. Once all tests have completed it either reports that all
tests passed, or prints the number of failed tests. Finally, it makes
several beeps. If a test fails, it can be run on its own by finding the
corresponding ROM in individual/.

Ths compact format on screen is to avoid having the results scroll off
the top, so the test can be started and allowed to run without having to
constantly monitor the display. 

Currently there is no well-defined way for an emulator test rig to
programatically find the result of the test; contact me if you're trying

Game Boy CPU Memory Access Timing Test
--------------------------------------
This ROM tests the timing of memory reads and writes made by
instructions, except stack and program counter accesses. These tests
require correct instruction timing and proper timer operation (TAC,
TIMA, TMA).

The read and write tests list failing instructions as

	[CB] opcode:tested-correct

The read-modify-write test lists failing instructions as 

	[CB] opcode:tested read/tested write-correct read/correct write

The values after the opcode refer to which instruction cycle the access
occurs on, with 1 being the first. If a time couldn't be determined due
to some other problem, it prints 0.

For instructions which either read or write, but not both, the CPU makes
the access on the last cycle. For instructions which read, modify, then
write back, the CPU reads on the next-to-last cycle, and writes on the
last cycle.


Internal operation
------------------
The tests have the timer increment TIMA every 64 cycles, synchronize
with this, delay a variable amount, then have the instruction under test
access the timer. By varying the delay in one-cycle increments, the
memory access made by the instruction can be made to fall before and
after a TIMA increment. By then examining the registers and value in
TIMA, it can be determined which occurred.


Multi-ROM
---------
In the main directory is a single ROM which runs all the tests. It
prints a test's number, runs the test, then "ok" if it passes, otherwise
a failure code. Once all tests have completed it either reports that all
tests passed, or prints the number of failed tests. Finally, it makes
several beeps. If a test fails, it can be run on its own by finding the
corresponding ROM in individual/.

Ths compact format on screen is to avoid having the results scroll off
the top, so the test can be started and allowed to run without having to
constantly monitor the display. 

Currently there is no well-defined way for an emulator test rig to
programatically find the result of the test; contact me if you're trying

This test measures relative timing between a sync point (reading TIMA in a loop) and a later access in the instruction being tested, both going through the same tick-then-access Bus::read path, so read-to-read ordering doesn't matter — though write timing is a separate case I need to consider.

Looking at the write test more carefully: it writes a value to TIMA, then checks afterward whether the periodic increment happened before or after the write, since both overwrite each other depending on which comes first in the cycle. Since the read/write access in cycle k always happens after that cycle's tick, both reads and writes see consistent post-tick state, so the model should be fine — though I want to double check the tima_64 sync file to confirm this holds when counting at 64 cycles rather than during an actual overflow.

I'm working through the sync routine logic: writing zero to TIMA then immediately reading it back to detect whether an increment happened within that narrow timing window, essentially probing the exact cycle alignment between the write and read operations.

The 65-cycle loop against a 64-cycle period means the phase drifts by one cycle each pass, eventually catching the increment right between the write and read. What matters is that the convention for "which cycle a write or read belongs to" stays consistent between the sync routine and the measurement itself, so the reported cycle index remains relative and self-consistent regardless of how real hardware defines it.

For instr_timing, the approach is similar but purely relative — durations are measured via start/stop timer calls at 4-cycle (M-cycle) granularity, so the D002 ordering question doesn't actually matter there either.

I do want to check the init_timer self-test more carefully though, since it's failing with error #255. I need to trace the exact M-cycle sequence of the delay/register-write/IF-check routine, so I should look at macros.inc and delay.s to understand how "delay", "wreg", and "lda" are implemented.

; This test rapidly starts and stops the timer.
; There are two behaviours that affect the test:
;   1. starting or stopping the timer does *not* reset its internal counter,
;      so repeated starting and stopping does not prevent timer increments
;   2. the timer circuit design causes some unexpected timer increases

; Common reasons for failing this test:
;   "FAIL: NO INTR"
;     Your emulator starts counting the timer when it is started or stopped.
;     This is incorrect, because in real hardware starting/stopping the timer
;     simply flips a single bit, and the timer state is otherwise preserved.
;   BC < $FFF8
;     Your emulator does not emulate the unexpected timer increases, so the
;     interrupt happens too late.

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2, CGB, AGB, AGS
;   fail: -

.include "common.s"

test:
  ld a, INTR_TIMER
  ldh (<IE), a
  xor a
  ldh (<IF), a
  ldh (<DIV), a
  ld a, $F0
  ldh (<TIMA), a
  ld a, %00000100 ; Start 4096 Hz timer
  ldh (<TAC), a

  ld bc, $FFFF

  ei

- ld a, %00000100 ; Start 4096 Hz timer
  ldh (<TAC), a
  ld a, %00000000 ; Stop timer
  ldh (<TAC), a
  dec bc
  ld a, c
  or b
  jr nz, -

  quit_failure_string "FAIL: NO INTR"

test_finish:
  setup_assertions
  assert_b $FF
  assert_c $D9
  quit_check_asserts

.org INTR_VEC_TIMER
  jp test_finish

Totaling the cycles gives 26 M-cycles to the SC write, placing the counter at 0xAC30 at that point. Since bit 8 is currently 0, I need to find when it next falls — that happens at the next multiple of 512, which is 464 T-cycles (116 M-cycles) later, and then seven more falling edges occur every 128 M-cycles after that.

So the eighth falling edge lands at 1012 M-cycles past the SC write, putting the IF set at absolute cycle 1038. Checking when the CPU's interrupt dispatch would see this flag, I count 1011 register increments before dispatch under both the before-fetch and late-sampling models, giving 144 full 7-register rounds plus 3 extra increments — but the expected result (A=0x12, B=0x91, C=0x90) only requires 1010 increments, so I'm still off by one somewhere, maybe due to a different edge or bit being used for the serial shift clock.

Recomputing the tick where bit 8 falls, I get IF raised at w+1012 which is tick 1038, so I need to check whether that's visible by cycle 1037's check-before-fetch or seen during fetch at 1038 to land on exactly 1010 increments.

Working through late-sampling: after inc #1010 at cycle 1037, the fetch for inc #1011 happens at cycle 1038, which is exactly when IF gets set, so the check after that fetch catches it and discards inc #1011, matching the expected 1010 increments. My earlier before-fetch attempt gave 1011 instead, so late-sampling is the model that fits — meaning both rapid_toggle and boot_sclk_align are consistent with late-sampling.

This points to a strong hypothesis: the CPU samples IF after the opcode-fetch M-cycle of the next instruction, due to hardware fetch/execute overlap, so peripheral interrupts raised during that cycle's tick get taken before the instruction executes. **What each part does:**
- **Bus:** the full memory map from the brief, plus I/O dispatch. Peripheral timing lives in one function, `Bus::tick`, in the order the brief specifies (D002).
- **Power-up state:** the internal timer counter starts at `0xABC8`, so DIV reads `0xAB`. The low byte is chosen so DIV ticks over at the moment the hardware does after boot. If T30 ever reverses the D002 order, this becomes `0xABCC` (there is a comment in `timer.rs`).
- **Timer:** falling-edge increments, extra increments from writes to DIV or TAC, and the one-M-cycle delay before the reload. Writes to TIMA/TMA during those cycles behave as Timer_Obscure_Behaviour.md describes.
- **Save state:** header is `GBEMUST`, version u16, and the 19-byte fingerprint, then the modules in the order you gave. The header is checked before anything changes. If loading the body fails, the machine is restored from a backup save, and leftover bytes at the end are rejected.

**New public items (D001 allows additions):**
- `Machine::rom_fingerprint()` and the constants `STATE_MAGIC`, `STATE_VERSION`, `FINGERPRINT_LEN`.
- `Timer::{reset_div, counter}`, `Serial::{take_output, transferring}`, `Joypad::set_buttons`, the `Interrupts` methods, and a `Snapshot` impl for Bus (its own state only).

**Small deviations from the brief:**
- FEA0–FEFF reads `0xFF` while OAM DMA is running (Pan Docs says so), otherwise `0x00`.

- **D021 SST 例外与 CPU 细则**（core T12/T14）：SST 500/500 文件、50 万用例通过；两项部分检查——`76 HALT`：SST 期望 3 M-cycle，本实现按 Opcodes.json 为 1（之后 halted 期间每次 step 1 个 idle），只比较寄存器/RAM/取指；`10 STOP`：SST 期望 PC+1 与 3 M-cycle，本实现按 Pan Docs/gbz80(7)/Opcodes.json 为 2 字节、1 M-cycle（第二字节跳过不读）并调用 `bus.stop()`（不进入低功耗，等同 2 字节 NOP），不比较 PC 与周期数。`Cpu` 新增公开字段 `ei_pending`/`halt_bug`/`locked` 与 `af/bc/de/hl` 访问器（不改冻结签名）。中断分派会取消挂起的 EI；`EI; HALT` 且已有挂起中断时触发 HALT bug；向量在写完 PCH 后决定（ie_push：IE 被清则 PC=0x0000、不 ack）；HALT 唤醒不额外耗时。

; This test checks all unused bits in working $FFxx IO,
; and all unused $FFxx IO. Unused bits and unused IO all return 1s.
; A test looks like this:
;
;            mask      write     expected
; test REG   MASK      WRITE     EXPECTED
;
;   1. write WRITE to REG
;   2. read VALUE from REG
;   3. compare VALUE & MASK with EXPECTED & MASK

; Verified results:
;   pass: DMG, MGB, SGB, SGB2
;   fail: CGB, AGB, AGS

.include "common.s"

.macro test ARGS reg mask write expect
  ld hl, _test_data_\@
  ld a, l
  ld (test_addr), a
  ld a, h
  ld (test_addr + 1), a

  ld sp, DEFAULT_SP

  call run_testcase
  jr _finish_\@

_test_data_\@:
  .db <reg
  .db mask
  .db write
  .db expect

; String representing bits in "write"
.repeat 8 INDEX bit
  .db '0' + (write >> (7 - bit)) & 1
.endr
  .db $00

; String representing bits in "expect"
; Bits not present in mask are spaces
.repeat 8 INDEX bit
  .if mask >> (7 - bit) & 1 != 0
    .db '0' + (expect >> (7 - bit)) & 1
  .else
    .db ' '
  .endif
.endr
  .db $00

_finish_\@:
.endm

; Simple unmapped all $00 and $FF tests
.macro test_unmapped
  test \1 %11111111 %00000000 %11111111
  test \1 %11111111 %11111111 %11111111
.endm

  di

  ;          mask      write     expected
  ;          |         |         |
  test P1    %11000000 %11111111 %11000000
  test P1    %11000000 %00111111 %11000000
  test SC    %01111110 %01111110 %01111110
  test SC    %01111110 %00000000 %01111110
  test TAC   %11111000 %11111000 %11111000
  test TAC   %11111000 %00000000 %11111000
  test IF    %11100000 %11100000 %11100000
  test IF    %11100000 %00000000 %11100000
  test STAT  %10000000 %10000000 %10000000
  test STAT  %10000000 %00000000 %10000000
  test NR10  %10000000 %00000000 %10000000
  test NR10  %10000000 %10000000 %10000000
  test NR30  %01111111 %00000000 %01111111
  test NR30  %01111111 %01111111 %01111111
  test NR32  %10011111 %00000000 %10011111
  test NR32  %10011111 %10011111 %10011111
  test NR41  %11000000 %00000000 %11000000
  test NR41  %11000000 %11000000 %11000000
  test NR44  %00111111 %00000000 %00111111
  test NR44  %00111111 %00111111 %00111111
  test NR52  %01110000 %10000000 %01110000
  test NR52  %01110000 %11110000 %01110000
  test IE    %11100000 %00000000 %00000000
  test IE    %11100000 %11100000 %11100000

  test_unmapped $FF03
  test_unmapped $FF08
  test_unmapped $FF09
  test_unmapped $FF0A
  test_unmapped $FF0B
  test_unmapped $FF0C
  test_unmapped $FF0D
  test_unmapped $FF0E
  test_unmapped $FF15
  test_unmapped $FF1F
  test_unmapped $FF27
  test_unmapped $FF28
  test_unmapped $FF29

; $FF4C - $FF7F
.repeat $34 INDEX offset
  test_unmapped $FF4C + offset
.endr

  quit_ok

; Inputs:
;   HL: test data address
run_testcase:
  ; C = reg
  ld a, (hl)
  ld c, a

  inc hl
  ; B = mask
  ld a, (hl)
  ld b, a

  ; write value to reg
  inc hl
  ld a, (hl)
  ld ($FF00+C), a

  ; read value, apply mask
  ld a, ($FF00+C)
  and b

  ; check expectation
  ld d, a
  inc hl
  ld a, (hl)
  and b
  cp d
  ret z

  ld a, d
  ld (test_got), a

  call fetch_test_data

  quit_inline
  print_string_literal "TEST FAILED"
  call print_newline
  call print_newline
  print_string_literal "$FF"

  ld a, (test_reg)
  call print_hex8

  print_string_literal "       76543210"
  call print_newline
  call print_newline
  print_string_literal "WROTE       "

  ld bc, test_str_write
  call print_string

  call print_newline
  print_string_literal "EXPECTED    "

  ld bc, test_str_expect
  call print_string

  call print_newline
  print_string_literal "GOT         "

  call print_got

  ld d, $42
  ret

fetch_test_data:
  ld a, (test_addr)
  ld e, a
  ld a, (test_addr + 1)

The IE register test checks that unused upper bits are writable and readable, which our implementation already handles correctly. But STAT's bit 7 is PPU territory — our stub stores it raw, so writing 0 won't clear it properly until the PPU lane implements forcing that bit high on reads.

I should check the ppu.rs state to see if that's handled, and also verify the unmapped register ranges (FF27-FF29, FF15, FF1F, FF4C-FF7F) all correctly return FF. For the APU register read masks, I want to pull the actual bit patterns from the Audio_Registers documentation rather than relying on memory.

1:# Audio Registers
15:One of the pitfalls of the `NRxy` naming convention is that the register's purpose is not immediately clear from its name, so some alternative `AUD*` names have been proposed, [such as `AUDENA` for `NR52`](https://github.com/gbdev/hardware.inc/blob/8d4432e5796bffe2e13c438013285c5f11c37b99/hardware.inc#L910).
17:## Global control registers
19:### FF26 — NR52: Audio master control
21:{{#bits 8 >
25:- **Audio on/off** (*Read/Write*): This controls whether the APU is powered on at all (akin to [`LCDC` bit 7](<#LCDC.7 — LCD enable>)).
26:  Turning the APU off drains less power (around 16%), but clears all APU registers and makes them read-only until turned back on, except `NR52`[^dmg_apu_off].
27:  Turning the APU off, however, does not affect [Wave RAM](<#FF30–FF3F — Wave pattern RAM>), which can always be read/written, nor the [DIV-APU](<#DIV-APU>) counter.
29:- **CH<var>n</var> on?** (*Read-only*): Each of these four bits allows checking whether channels are active[^nr52_dac].
32:  A channel is turned on by triggering it (i.e. setting bit 7 of `NRx4`)[^dac_off].
34:      - The channel's [length timer](<#Length timer>) is enabled in `NRx4` and expires, or
35:      - *For CH1 only*: when the [period sweep](<#FF10 — NR10: Channel 1 sweep>) overflows[^freq_sweep_underflow], or
36:      - [The channel's DAC](#DACs) is turned off.
42:[^dmg_apu_off]:
45:[^nr52_dac]:
46:Actually, only the status of the channels' *generation* circuits is reported, not the status of [the DACs](#DACs). A channel can only be ON if its corresponding DAC is, though.
48:[^dac_off]:
49:If [the channel's DAC](#DACs) is off, then the write to NRx4 will be ineffective and won't turn the channel on.
51:[^freq_sweep_underflow]:
54:### FF25 — NR51: Sound panning
58:{{#bits 8 >
64:Note that selecting or de-selecting a channel whose [DAC](#DACs) is enabled will [cause an audio pop](#Mixer).
66:### FF24 — NR50: Master volume & VIN panning
68:{{#bits 8 >
72:- **VIN left/right**: These work exactly like the bits in [`NR51`](<#FF25 — NR51: Sound panning>). They should be set at 0 if external sound hardware is not being used.
78:## Sound Channel 1 — Pulse with period sweep
80:### FF10 — NR10: Channel 1 sweep
84:{{#bits 8 >
88:- **Pace**: This dictates how often sweep "iterations" happen, in units of 128 Hz ticks[^div_apu] (7.8 ms).
89:  Note that the value written to this field is not re-read by the hardware until a sweep iteration completes, or the channel is [(re)triggered](<#Triggering>).
99:On each sweep iteration, the period in [`NR13`](<#FF13 — NR13: Channel 1 period low \[write-only\]>) and [`NR14`](<#FF14 — NR14: Channel 1 period high & control>) is modified and written back.
107:[^div_apu]:
108:[As long as `DIV` is not written to](#DIV-APU).
110:### FF11 — NR11: Channel 1 length timer & duty cycle
112:This register controls both the channel's [length timer](<#Length timer>) and [duty cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duty_cycle) (the ratio of the time spent low vs. high).
129:{{#bits 8 >
133:- **Duty cycle** (*Read/Write*): Controls the output waveform as follows:
143:- **Initial length timer** (*Write-only*): The higher this field is, [the shorter the time before the channel is cut](<#Length timer>).
145:### FF12 — NR12: Channel 1 volume & envelope
149:{{#bits 8 >
157:Setting bits 3-7 of this register all to 0 (initial volume = 0, envelope = decreasing) turns the DAC off (and thus, the channel as well), which [may cause an audio pop](<#Mixer>).
161:Writes to this register while the channel is on require retriggering it afterwards.
166:### FF13 — NR13: Channel 1 period low \[write-only\]
168:This register stores the low 8 bits of the channel's 11-bit "[period value](<#Frequency>)".
197:([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_1/channel_1_freq_change.asm))
201:### FF14 — NR14: Channel 1 period high & control
203:{{#bits 8 >
207:- **Trigger** (*Write-only*): Writing any value to `NR14` with this bit set [triggers](<#Triggering>) the channel, causing the
214:  * Sweep does [several things](<#Pulse channel with sweep (CH1)>).
216:- **[Length](<#Length timer>) enable** (*Read/Write*): Takes effect immediately upon writing to this register.
217:- **Period** (*Write-only*): The upper 3 bits of the period value; the lower 8 bits are stored in [`NR13`](<#FF13 — NR13: Channel 1 period low \[write-only\]>).
219:## Sound Channel 2 — Pulse
221:This sound channel works exactly like channel 1, except that it lacks a period sweep (and thus an equivalent to [`NR10`](<#FF10 — NR10: Channel 1 sweep>)).
223:- `NR21` (\$FF16) → [`NR11`](<#FF11 — NR11: Channel 1 length timer & duty cycle>)
224:- `NR22` (\$FF17) → [`NR12`](<#FF12 — NR12: Channel 1 volume & envelope>)
225:- `NR23` (\$FF18) → [`NR13`](<#FF13 — NR13: Channel 1 period low \[write-only\]>)
226:- `NR24` (\$FF19) → [`NR14`](<#FF14 — NR14: Channel 1 period high & control>)
228:## Sound Channel 3 — Wave output
237:### FF1A — NR30: Channel 3 DAC enable
239:This register controls CH3's [DAC](#DACs).
242:{{#bits 8 >
246:The DAC is often turned off just before writing to [wave RAM](<#FF30–FF3F — Wave pattern RAM>) to avoid issues with accessing it; see further below for more info.
248:Turning the DAC off [may cause an audio pop](<#Mixer>).
250:### FF1B — NR31: Channel 3 length timer \[write-only\]
252:This register controls the channel's [length timer](<#Length timer>).
254:{{#bits 8 >
258:The higher the [length timer](<#Length timer>), the shorter the time before the channel is cut.
260:### FF1C — NR32: Channel 3 output level
264:{{#bits 8 >
277:### FF1D — NR33: Channel 3 period low \[write-only\]
279:This register stores the low 8 bits of the channel's 11-bit "[period value](<#Frequency>)".
298:([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_freq_change_delay.asm))
302:### FF1E — NR34: Channel 3 period high & control
304:{{#bits 8 >
308:- **Trigger** (*Write-only*): Writing any value to `NR34` with this bit set [triggers](<#Triggering>) the channel, causing the
325:    ([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_delay.asm))
329:- **[Length](<#Length timer>) enable** (*Read/Write*): Takes effect immediately upon writing to this register.
330:- **Period** (*Write-only*): The upper 3 bits of the period value; the lower 8 bits are stored in [`NR33`](<#FF1D — NR33: Channel 3 period low \[write-only\]>).
332:### FF30–FF3F — Wave pattern RAM
342:([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_first_sample.asm))
348:- On AGB, reads return $FF, and writes are ignored. ([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_wave_ram_locked_write.asm))
351:- On other consoles, the byte accessed will be the one CH3 is currently reading[^wave_access]; that is, if CH3 is currently reading one of the first two samples, the CPU will really access $FF30, regardless of the address being used. ([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_wave_ram_locked_write.asm))
353:Wave RAM *can* be accessed normally even if the DAC is on, as long as the channel is not active. ([Source](https://github.com/LIJI32/SameSuite/blob/master/apu/channel_3/channel_3_wave_ram_dac_on_rw.asm))
354:This is especially relevant on GBA, whose [mixer behaves as if DACs are always enabled](<#Game Boy Advance audio>).
356:[^wave_access]:
360:## Sound Channel 4 — Noise
362:This channel is used to output white noise[^not_white], which is done by randomly switching the amplitude between two levels fairly fast.
369:[^not_white]:
372:### FF20 — NR41: Channel 4 length timer \[write-only\]
374:This register controls the channel's [length timer](<#Length timer>).
376:{{#bits 8 >

I'm defining the read-mask table for the APU registers FF10–FF2F, where unused bits read as 1 per Pan Docs, while the waveform RAM region FF30–FF3F uses a zero mask for normal read/write access.

Now I'm thinking through NR52's write behavior — toggling bit 7 powers the APU on/off, with status bits 0-3 being read-only, and considering whether to implement full power-off register clearing as described in Pan Docs, weighing whether games like Pokémon actually rely on this behavior enough to justify the complexity.

The DMG exception complicates things further: length timers in NRx1 remain writable even while the APU is powered off, but since duty bits share the same register as length bits in NR11/NR21, I need to figure out whether writes while powered off should still affect the duty cycle or only the length portion.

Given this is only observable through register reads, not actual sound, I'm questioning whether handling power-off register clearing falls outside the stated scope of implementing read-masking without sound generation. It's cheap to implement and well-documented, but untested by the test ROMs I'm targeting, so leaving it out keeps things simpler without audible consequences for games that write other sound registers before enabling the APU.

I also realize the existing bus test that writes 0x3C to various sound registers and expects it back will now fail since masked registers won't round-trip that value — I need to update that test to account for the new masking behavior.
